blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 13 (Halogens), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 What are halogens? Name the common members of the family.
blocks.explanation: Halogens are the elements of Group 17 (VIIA) of the periodic table: a group of very reactive non-metals with similar chemical properties. The common members are fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine; astatine and tennessine are very rare and radioactive.

book_ref.quote: Elements present in Group 17 or VIIA of the periodic table are termed as halogens

blocks.prompt: 2 How did the halogens get their name?
blocks.explanation: The name comes from the Greek words 'halos', meaning salt, and 'gen', meaning to make; so halogen means salt maker.

book_ref.quote: meaning “salt”, and “gen”, meaning “to make.”

blocks.prompt: 3 State the physical state and colour of each common halogen at room temperature.
blocks.explanation: All exist as diatomic molecules. F₂: pale yellow gas; Cl₂: greenish yellow gas; Br₂: volatile reddish-brown liquid with corrosive, toxic fumes; I₂: shiny greyish black solid that sublimes to a violet vapour.

book_ref.quote: Halogens exist as diatomic molecules in all phases (gas, liquid or solid)

blocks.prompt: 4 Why do the colours of the halogens darken from chlorine to iodine?
blocks.explanation: The colour darkens progressively because the absorption of light changes as a result of electron transitions within the molecules of the respective halogens.

book_ref.quote: due to changes in the absorption of light as a result of electron transitions

blocks.prompt: 5 Chlorine is poisonous. Is it of any use to the human body?
blocks.explanation: Yes. Although chlorine is poisonous, a small amount is essential to human health and life in the form of chloride.

book_ref.quote: small amount is essential to human health and life in the form of chloride

blocks.prompt: 6 Write the electron shell structure and outer shell configuration of chlorine and iodine (Table 13.1).
blocks.explanation: Chlorine (Z = 17): 2, 8, 7; outer shell 3s²3p⁵. Iodine (Z = 53): 2, 8, 18, 18, 7; outer shell 5s²5p⁵. Both have seven outer-shell electrons.

book_ref.quote: Outer shell electron configuration

blocks.text: 13.1 Volatility of chlorine, bromine and iodine

blocks.prompt: 7 Arrange chlorine, bromine and iodine in order of decreasing volatility and give the state of each at room temperature.
blocks.explanation: Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. Chlorine is a gas (it disperses quickly in air), bromine is a liquid that evaporates readily giving toxic fumes, and iodine is a solid, the least volatile.

book_ref.quote: At room temperature chlorine is a gas (bromine is the liquid and iodine a solid)

blocks.prompt: 8 Give three reasons why volatility decreases from chlorine to iodine.
blocks.explanation: Down the group: (i) molecular mass increases; (ii) the size of the outer shell increases; (iii) intermolecular forces (London dispersion forces) become stronger. Stronger forces hold the molecules together, so volatility falls.

book_ref.quote: This trend is due to the increasing molecular mass, increase in size of outer shell and stronger intermolecular forces

blocks.prompt: 9 Why is bromine named from the Greek word 'bromos'?
blocks.explanation: 'Bromos' means stench. Bromine liquid evaporates easily at room temperature giving an orange vapour with a very strong and bad odour.

book_ref.quote: Bromine has a very strong and bad odor.

blocks.text: 13.2 Trend in volatility of the halogens

blocks.prompt: 10 Which intermolecular forces act between halogen molecules, and why only these?
blocks.explanation: Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id or London dispersion) forces. Halogen molecules X₂ are non-polar (two identical atoms), so they have no permanent dipoles; only temporary dipoles attract them.

book_ref.quote: Halogens are non-polar and instantaneous dipole-induced forces play a significant role

blocks.prompt: 11 How are volatility and boiling point related? Explain with a reason.
blocks.explanation: Volatility is inversely related to boiling point: a more volatile substance has a lower boiling point. Stronger intermolecular forces need more energy to separate molecules from liquid to gas, raising the boiling point and lowering volatility.

book_ref.quote: Volatility is inversely related to the boiling point of a substance.

blocks.prompt: 12 Differentiate between small and large halogen molecules in their London forces and physical properties (Table 13.2).
blocks.explanation: Small molecules have weak forces and are more volatile; large molecules have strong forces and are less volatile:

book_ref.quote: Table 13.2 Effect of London forces on physical properties

blocks.prompt: 13 Why is chlorine a gas while iodine is a solid at room temperature?
blocks.explanation: Chlorine molecules are small with weak id-id forces, so they stay apart as a gas. Iodine molecules are the largest and most polarizable, with the strongest forces in the group, so iodine is a solid.

book_ref.quote: Iodine has the strongest forces among the group, so it is in solid state at room temperature.

blocks.prompt: 14 Using Table 13.1, find the difference between the boiling points of iodine and bromine and explain it.
blocks.explanation: b.p. of I₂ = 183 °C, Br₂ = 59 °C; difference = 183 - 59 = 124 °C. Iodine molecules are larger and more polarizable, so their London forces are stronger and more energy is needed to boil it.

book_ref.quote: The forces depend on factors like molecular size, shape and polarizability

blocks.text: 13.3 The bond strength of halogen molecules

blocks.prompt: 15 Why does the X-X bond energy decrease from chlorine to iodine?
blocks.explanation: Atomic size increases down the group, so the bond length becomes longer and the bond weaker: Cl₂ 243, Br₂ 193, I₂ 151 kJ mol⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: increase in the atomic size down the group which results in longer bond lengths and weaker bonds

blocks.prompt: 16 Justify: the F-F bond is weaker than the Cl-Cl bond although fluorine is more electronegative.
blocks.explanation: Fluorine atoms are very small, so the lone pairs on the two bonded atoms are close together and repel strongly. This electron-electron repulsion weakens the bond: F₂ 156 kJ mol⁻¹ against Cl₂ 243 kJ mol⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: significant electron–electron repulsion between the lone pairs on the fluorine atoms

blocks.prompt: 17 Arrange F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂ in decreasing order of bond energy with values.
blocks.explanation: Cl₂ (243) > Br₂ (193) > F₂ (156) > I₂ (151) kJ mol⁻¹. Fluorine is out of order because of lone-pair repulsion in its small atoms.

book_ref.quote: Table 13.3 Bond energies of halogen molecules

blocks.prompt: 18 From Table 13.3, calculate how much the bond energy falls from Cl₂ to Br₂ and from Br₂ to I₂.
blocks.explanation: Cl₂ → Br₂: 243 - 193 = 50 kJ mol⁻¹. Br₂ → I₂: 193 - 151 = 42 kJ mol⁻¹. The bond energy decreases gradually down the group.

book_ref.quote: Moving from top to bottom in group 17, the bond energy of halogens decreases gradually from chlorine to iodine.

blocks.text: 13.4 Relative reactivities of the halogens as oxidising agents

blocks.prompt: 19 Why do halogens act as oxidizing agents? Give one equation.
blocks.explanation: Halogens gain electrons from metals and most non-metals and become negative halide ions, so they oxidize the other element. Example: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s).

book_ref.quote: All the free halogens act as oxidizing agents when they react with metals and most of non-metals.

blocks.prompt: 20 Write the balanced equations for fluorine displacing bromide and iodide ions.
blocks.explanation:
F₂(g) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2F⁻(aq) + Br₂
F₂(g) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2F⁻(aq) + I₂
One F₂ takes two electrons from two halide ions and gives two fluoride ions.

book_ref.quote: The balanced equations are F₂(g) + 2Cl¹⁻(aq) → 2F¹⁻(aq) + Cl₂(g)

blocks.prompt: 21 Which halide ions can chlorine displace? Give a balanced ionic equation for one.
blocks.explanation: Chlorine can oxidize and displace Br⁻ and I⁻ (not F⁻). Example: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.

book_ref.quote: Similarly, chlorine can oxidize and displace Br⁻ and I⁻.

blocks.prompt: 22 Give reason: iodine cannot displace any other halide ion from its solution.
blocks.explanation: Iodine is the weakest oxidizing agent among the halogens (lowest E°, +0.54 V). A halogen displaces only the halide ions below it, and no common halogen lies below iodine.

book_ref.quote: Iodine cannot oxidize any halide ion.

blocks.prompt: 23 How do the E° (X₂/X⁻) values show the trend in oxidizing power? Quote the values.
blocks.explanation: E° becomes less positive from F₂ to I₂: F₂ +2.87 V, Cl₂ +1.36 V, Br₂ +1.07 V, I₂ +0.54 V. The less positive the E°, the weaker the oxidizing power, so F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

book_ref.quote: The oxidizing power of halogens can be related to standard electrode potential (E°) values.

blocks.prompt: 24 Name the factors on which the oxidizing power of a halogen depends.
blocks.explanation: Energy of dissociation, electron affinity of the atoms, hydration energy of the ions and heat of vaporization (for Br₂ and I₂). Low dissociation energy, high electron affinity and high hydration energy give high oxidizing power.

book_ref.quote: energy of dissociation, electron affinity of atoms, hydration energies of ions, and heats of vaporization

blocks.prompt: 25 Using Table 13.4, by how much does E° fall from F₂ to I₂? What does it show?
blocks.explanation: 2.87 - 0.54 = 2.33 V. The large fall shows that fluorine is by far the most powerful oxidizing agent and iodine the weakest.

book_ref.quote: Table 13.4 Standard electrode potential E° (X₂/X⁻)

blocks.text: 13.5 Reactions of the halogens with hydrogen

blocks.prompt: 26 Write the general equation for the reaction of halogens with hydrogen and state the order of reactivity.
blocks.explanation: H₂ + X₂ → 2HX, where X₂ = F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ or I₂. Reactivity with hydrogen decreases down the group: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

book_ref.quote: When halogen elements react with hydrogen, they produce hydrogen halides.

blocks.prompt: 27 Write the conditions and equations for the reactions of fluorine and chlorine with hydrogen.
blocks.explanation: Fluorine reacts explosively even at low temperature in the dark: H₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2HF(g). Chlorine reacts readily in UV light (hν) or with a spark: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g).

book_ref.quote: In the presence of UV light or a spark, chlorine reacts readily with hydrogen

blocks.prompt: 28 Differentiate between the reactions of bromine and iodine with hydrogen.
blocks.explanation: Both need heat, but iodine needs a catalyst too and its reaction is reversible:

book_ref.quote: At high temperature and in presence of a catalyst, iodine reacts with hydrogen

rows: Needs high temperature and a catalyst
HBr gives hydrobromic acid in water
HI gives hydroiodic acid in water

blocks.prompt: 29 What are hydrohalic acids? Name the acid formed by each hydrogen halide.
blocks.explanation: Hydrogen halides are colourless gases that dissolve in water to give hydrohalic acids: HF → hydrofluoric acid, HCl → hydrochloric acid, HBr → hydrobromic acid, HI → hydroiodic acid.

book_ref.quote: Hydrogen halides are colourless gases that dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acid.

blocks.prompt: 30 Using Table 13.1 and H = 1, how many grams of HI can form at most from 2.538 g of iodine? Why is the actual yield lower?
blocks.explanation: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. Moles I₂ = 2.538/253.8 = 0.01 mol; HI = 0.02 mol × 127.9 g mol⁻¹ = 2.558 g at most. The reaction is reversible and very slow, so iodine is not completely converted.

book_ref.quote: This is a reversible reaction and occurs very slowly.

blocks.text: 13.6 Relative thermal stabilities of hydrogen halides in terms of their bond strength

blocks.prompt: 31 Give the bond dissociation energies of the H-X bonds and the resulting order of thermal stability.
blocks.explanation: H-F 569, H-Cl 431, H-Br 366, H-I 299 kJ mol⁻¹. The stronger the bond, the more thermally stable the halide: HF > HCl > HBr > HI.

book_ref.quote: The bond dissociation energy of H-F (569 kJ/mol) is the highest among the hydrogen halides.

blocks.prompt: 32 How does orbital overlap explain the weaker H-Br bond compared with H-Cl?
blocks.explanation: Bromine has a larger atomic radius than chlorine, so overlap between the hydrogen and bromine orbitals is reduced. The H-Br bond (366 kJ mol⁻¹) is therefore weaker than H-Cl (431 kJ mol⁻¹).

book_ref.quote: There is a reduced overlapping of orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 33 Differentiate between HF and HI with respect to bond and thermal stability.
blocks.explanation: HF is the most and HI the least thermally stable hydrogen halide:

book_ref.quote: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) is the most thermally stable hydrogen halide.

rows: Very large iodine atom, low electronegativity

blocks.prompt: 34 Using Table 13.5, find the energy needed to break all the H-X bonds in 0.5 mol of HCl and in 0.5 mol of HI.
blocks.explanation: HCl: 0.5 × 431 = 215.5 kJ. HI: 0.5 × 299 = 149.5 kJ. Less energy breaks HI, so it decomposes more easily on heating.

book_ref.quote: Table 13.5 Bond dissociation energy of H-X bonds

blocks.text: 13.7 Relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents

blocks.prompt: 35 Arrange the halide ions in decreasing reducing power and state the two properties responsible.
blocks.explanation: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻. Down the group electronegativity decreases and ionic size increases, so charge density falls and the ion gives up an electron more easily.

book_ref.quote: The order of decreasing power as a reducing agent is I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻.

blocks.prompt: 36 Why is the fluoride ion the weakest reducing agent?
blocks.explanation: Fluorine is highly electronegative and holds its extra electron strongly. F⁻ is small with a high charge density, which stabilizes it, so it has very little tendency to lose an electron.

book_ref.quote: the strong bond between the fluorine atom and its extra electron make it difficult

blocks.prompt: 37 What is meant by charge density, and how does it affect the reducing power of the iodide ion?
blocks.explanation: Charge density is the charge compared with the size of the ion. The iodide ion is large, so its single negative charge is spread out (low charge density); its electron is held loosely and is donated easily, making I⁻ a strong reducing agent.

book_ref.quote: This results in a lower charge density and a tendency to donate an electron by the iodide ion

blocks.prompt: 38 Differentiate between bromide and fluoride ions as reducing agents.
blocks.explanation: Bromide is the stronger reducing agent:

book_ref.quote: Bromide ion (Br⁻) has a larger ionic radius and lower charge density

rows: Loses an electron easily; stronger reducing agent
Hardly loses an electron; weakest reducing agent

blocks.text: 13.8 Reactions of halides with aqueous silver ion followed by aqueous ammonia

blocks.prompt: 39 What is the silver nitrate test? Write its correct general ionic equation.
blocks.explanation: A test for halide ions: aqueous AgNO₃ is added and the colour of the insoluble silver halide shows the halide. General equation: X⁻(aq) + Ag⁺(aq) → AgX(s).

book_ref.quote: These reactions are used in qualitative analysis to identify halides ions.

blocks.prompt: 40 Why can the silver nitrate test not detect fluoride ions by a precipitate?
blocks.explanation: Silver fluoride is soluble in water, so no precipitate forms and no reaction is visible when Ag⁺ and F⁻ are mixed.

book_ref.quote: As silver fluoride is soluble in water, Fluoride (F⁻) does not form precipitate as silver fluoride.

blocks.prompt: 41 Write the ionic equations and the colours of the precipitates formed by Ag⁺(aq) with chloride and iodide ions.
blocks.explanation:
Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s), white precipitate.
Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s), yellow precipitate.

book_ref.quote: a white precipitate of silver chloride forms, which is soluble in dilute ammonia

blocks.prompt: 42 Using Ag = 108 and Table 13.1 (Na = 23), find the mass of AgBr precipitated from 2.058 g of NaBr with excess AgNO₃.
blocks.explanation: NaBr = 23 + 79.9 = 102.9 g mol⁻¹; moles = 2.058/102.9 = 0.02 mol. Ag⁺ + Br⁻ → AgBr, so AgBr = 0.02 mol × 187.9 g mol⁻¹ = 3.758 g.

book_ref.quote: This type of reactions is used to identify halide ions and is called silver nitrate test.

blocks.prompt: 43 Why is aqueous ammonia added after silver nitrate in testing halides?
blocks.explanation: The white, cream and yellow precipitates can look alike. Ammonia tests their solubility: AgCl dissolves in dilute NH₃, AgBr only in concentrated NH₃ and AgI in neither, which confirms the halide.

book_ref.quote: Addition of aqueous ammonia tests the solubility of initially formed silver halide precipitates.

blocks.prompt: 44 Write the equation for silver chloride dissolving in ammonia and name the complex ion formed.
blocks.explanation: AgCl(s) + 2NH₃(aq) → [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). The complex ion [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ is the diamminesilver(I) ion; the solution is colourless.

book_ref.quote: The white precipitate of AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia forming a colourless solution.

blocks.prompt: 45 Differentiate between silver chloride and silver bromide.
blocks.explanation: Both are insoluble silver halides but differ in colour and in solubility in ammonia:

book_ref.quote: The cream-coloured precipitate of AgBr dissolves in concentrated ammonia

rows: Soluble only in concentrated aqueous ammonia

blocks.prompt: 46 A solution gives a pale yellow precipitate with AgNO₃(aq) which does not dissolve in concentrated ammonia. Identify the halide ion and write the equation.
blocks.explanation: The halide ion is iodide, I⁻. Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s); silver iodide does not dissolve in dilute or concentrated ammonia.

book_ref.quote: does not dissolve in both dilute and concentrated ammonia

blocks.text: 13.9 Reactions of halides (X-) with concentrated sulfuric acid

blocks.prompt: 47 Write the equation for concentrated sulfuric acid with sodium fluoride. Why does the reaction stop at HF?
blocks.explanation: NaF(s) + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄ + HF(g); fumes of HF are seen. HF is a weak reducing agent, so it cannot reduce H₂SO₄ and does not react further.

book_ref.quote: Fumes of hydrogen fluoride gas are produced when concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with NaF.

blocks.prompt: 48 Write the two equations for the reaction of sodium bromide with concentrated sulfuric acid.
blocks.explanation:
NaBr + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄ + HBr(g)
2HBr(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → Br₂(g) + SO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)
In the second step HBr reduces the acid to SO₂ and is oxidized to Br₂.

book_ref.quote: Hydrogen bromide acts as a reducing agent by reducing sulfuric acid to sulfur dioxide and is self-oxidized to bromine.

blocks.prompt: 49 Show the change in oxidation states of iodine and sulfur in the reaction of HI with concentrated sulfuric acid.
blocks.explanation: 8HI(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → 4I₂(s) + H₂S(g) + 4H₂O(l). Iodine: -1 (HI) → 0 (I₂), oxidized. Sulfur: +6 (H₂SO₄) → -2 (H₂S), reduced by 8 units; 8 I atoms each lose one electron.

book_ref.quote: 8HI(g) + H₂SO₄(l) → 4I₂(s) + H₂S(g) + 4H₂O(l)

blocks.prompt: 50 Differentiate between the reactions of concentrated sulfuric acid with NaCl and with NaI.
blocks.explanation: Chloride gives only HCl; iodide goes on to a redox reaction:

book_ref.quote: When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with sodium chloride, fumes of hydrogen chloride gas are produced.

rows: Fumes of HI, purple fumes of iodine, smell of H₂S
NaI + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HI, then 8HI + H₂SO₄ → 4I₂ + H₂S + 4H₂O
Redox: HI reduces H₂SO₄ to H₂S

blocks.prompt: 51 Why do the reactions of halides with concentrated sulfuric acid become more complex from fluoride to iodide?
blocks.explanation: Reducing power increases from F⁻ to I⁻. HF and HCl cannot reduce the acid; HBr reduces it to SO₂ (S +6 → +4) and HI, the strongest, reduces it further to H₂S (S +6 → -2).

book_ref.quote: leads to more complex reactions with concentrated sulfuric acid

blocks.text: 13.10 Reactions of chlorine with cold and hot aqueous sodium hydroxide

blocks.prompt: 52 What decides whether chlorine forms NaClO or NaClO₃ with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
blocks.explanation: The temperature of the reaction: cold aqueous NaOH gives NaCl and NaClO (sodium chlorate(I)); hot aqueous NaOH gives NaCl and NaClO₃ (sodium chlorate(V)).

book_ref.quote: form different products according to the temperature of the reaction

blocks.prompt: 53 Give the new and old names of NaClO and the oxidation state of chlorine in it.
blocks.explanation: New name: sodium chlorate(I); old name: sodium hypochlorite. Chlorine is +1 (Na +1, O -2: +1 + x - 2 = 0, x = +1).

book_ref.quote: Sodium chlorate (I) is previously called sodium hypochlorite.

blocks.prompt: 54 Using Table 13.1 and Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1, find the mass of NaOH needed to react completely with 3.55 g of chlorine in the cold.
blocks.explanation: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. Moles Cl₂ = 3.55/71.0 = 0.05 mol; NaOH = 2 × 0.05 = 0.1 mol; mass = 0.1 × 40 = 4.0 g.

book_ref.quote: The above reaction shows the simultaneous oxidation and reduction of chlorine

blocks.prompt: 55 In the balanced reaction of chlorine with hot NaOH, show that the electrons lost equal the electrons gained.
blocks.explanation: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O. Five Cl atoms go 0 → -1, gaining 5 × 1 = 5 electrons; one Cl atom goes 0 → +5, losing 5 electrons. 5 gained = 5 lost.

book_ref.quote: five Cl atoms are reduced to -1 and one is oxidised to +5

blocks.prompt: 56 Differentiate between the reactions of chlorine with cold and with hot aqueous NaOH.
blocks.explanation: Both are disproportionation reactions, but the products and oxidation states differ:

book_ref.quote: Chlorine is oxidized from 0 to +5 in NaClO₃.

blocks.text: 13.11 Use of chlorine in water purification

blocks.prompt: 57 Chlorine gas is very poisonous, yet it is added to drinking water. Explain.
blocks.explanation: In small quantities chlorine is harmless to humans but poisonous to disease-causing bacteria. Because of its strong disinfectant properties it is widely used at water treatment plants, where it forms active species (HOCl, OCl⁻) that kill pathogens.

book_ref.quote: Chlorine gas is very poisonous.

blocks.prompt: 58 Why is swimming-pool water given a slightly higher chlorine concentration than drinking water?
blocks.explanation: Swimming-pool water is likely to contain a higher concentration of bacteria, so slightly more chlorine is needed to disinfect it.

book_ref.quote: Water in the swimming pools is also chlorinated

blocks.prompt: 59 Write the equations showing how chlorine in water forms the chlorate(I) ion.
blocks.explanation:
Cl₂(g) + H₂O(l) → HCl(aq) + HClO(aq)
HOCl is a weak acid and partially dissociates: HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻ (chlorate(I) ion).

book_ref.quote: is a weak acid and partially dissociate in water

blocks.prompt: 60 Give reason: HOCl is a more effective disinfectant than OCl⁻.
blocks.explanation: HOCl has no charge (neutral), so it penetrates the cell walls of micro-organisms easily; the charged OCl⁻ ion does so less easily.

book_ref.quote: The neutral charge of HOCl allows to penetrate the cell walls of micro-organisms easily.

blocks.prompt: 61 Name three cell parts attacked by HOCl and OCl⁻ and state the result.
blocks.explanation: Proteins and lipids are oxidized, enzymes needed for survival and replication are inactivated, and nucleic acids (DNA, RNA) are oxidized. Cell function is disrupted, the bacteria cannot replicate and the cell dies.

book_ref.quote: can oxidize and inactivate enzymes that are crucial for survival and replication of bacteria

blocks.prompt: 62 How does pH affect the disinfection of water by chlorine?
blocks.explanation: At pH about 6-7.5, HOCl predominates and disinfection is more effective. Above pH 7.5, OCl⁻ predominates; it is less effective but still disinfects.

book_ref.quote: At higher pH (above 7.5), OCl⁻ predominates, its less effective but still provides disinfection.

blocks.prompt: 63 Why must the contact time of water with chlorine be long enough?
blocks.explanation: The disinfectants HOCl and OCl⁻ need time to penetrate and kill bacteria, viruses and protozoa; too short a contact leaves some micro-organisms alive.

book_ref.quote: to allow the disinfectants to penetrate and kill bacteria, viruses and protozoa
